questions.question: What is the Iron Age considered to be in the three-age system of technology?
options: The final epoch after the Copper Age and Bronze Age
The first epoch before the Stone Age
The middle epoch between the Stone Age and Bronze Age
A modern technological period after the Industrial Age
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states that the Iron Age is the final epoch of the three-age system of technology after the Copper Age and Bronze Age.
Incorrect. The Iron Age is not the first epoch before the Stone Age; it comes last.
Incorrect. The Iron Age is not the middle epoch between the Stone Age and Bronze Age; it follows both.
Incorrect. The article does not describe the Iron Age as a modern period after the Industrial Age.

questions.question: Which regions did the three-age system concepts originate for describing?
options: Iron Age Europe and the ancient Near East
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states these concepts originated for describing Iron Age Europe and the ancient Near East.
Incorrect. The article notes the Americas used a five-period system instead.
Incorrect. Sub-Saharan Africa and East Asia are not identified as the origin regions.
Incorrect. South America and Central Asia are not mentioned as the origin regions.

questions.question: When did the Iron Age begin in Anatolia, the Caucasus, or Southeast Europe?
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states the Iron Age began c. 1300 BC in Anatolia, the Caucasus, or Southeast Europe.
Incorrect. c. 5th century BC is when Northern Europe was reached.
Incorrect. c. 12th century BC refers to the ancient Near East transition.
Incorrect. c. 900 BC is not given as the start date for these regions.

questions.question: What defines the beginning of the Iron Age locally around the world?
options: When smelted iron production replaces bronze equivalents in common use
When meteoric iron artifacts are first discovered
When the Roman Empire conquers a region
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states the beginning is defined by archaeological convention when smelted iron production replaces bronze equivalents in common use.
Incorrect. Written history is discussed regarding the end of the Iron Age, not its beginning.
Incorrect. Meteoric iron was used for millennia before the Iron Age and does not define its start.
Incorrect. Roman conquest marks the end of the Iron Age in Central and Western Europe, not its beginning.

questions.question: What did indigenous cultures in the Americas not develop in the pre-Columbian era?
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states indigenous cultures in the Americas did not develop an iron economy in the pre-Columbian era.
Incorrect. The article does not state they lacked written language.
Incorrect. Stone tool technology is not mentioned as absent.
Incorrect. The article notes some indigenous cultures did work copper and silver.

questions.question: When did the Iron Age reach Northern Europe?
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states Northern Europe was not reached until c. the 5th century BC.
Incorrect. c. 1300 BC refers to Anatolia, the Caucasus, or Southeast Europe.
Incorrect. c. 1200 BC refers to the ancient Near East and spread to South Asia.
Incorrect. c. AD 800 marks the end of the Germanic Iron Age in Scandinavia.

questions.question: What is the traditional end date for the Iron Age in the ancient Near East?
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states the establishment of the Achaemenid Empire c. 550 BC is used traditionally as an end date.
Incorrect. c. AD 800 marks the end of the Germanic Iron Age in Scandinavia.
Incorrect. c. 1 BC marks the end of the Iron Age in Central and Western Europe.
Incorrect. c. 1200 BC marks the beginning of the Iron Age in the ancient Near East.

questions.question: What marks the end of the Iron Age in Central and Western Europe?
options: The conquests by the Roman Empire during the 1st century BC
The beginning of the Viking Age
The establishment of the Achaemenid Empire
answer_explanations: Correct. The article states Roman Empire conquests during the 1st century BC mark the end of the Iron Age in Central and Western Europe.
Incorrect. The Viking Age beginning c. AD 800 ends the Germanic Iron Age in Scandinavia.
Incorrect. The Achaemenid Empire c. 550 BC ends the Iron Age in the ancient Near East.
Incorrect. Written history is not cited as the end marker for Central and Western Europe.
